opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it was just my personality and part of it was the moment we were in. Back then, around 2012 or so, I was doing research on things like restricted Boltzmann machines and other deep learning models, and yes, Theano existed, and Alex Krizhevsky's CUDA ConvNet was out there. But for me, the way I really understand something is by building it myself. If I just call into a library, I can get a result, but I don't really know what's happening underneath: how the memory is laid out, why one kernel is fast and another is slow, where the bottlenecks actually are.

So I would write my own GPU code, my own little matrix libraries, sometimes in C++ with templates, which later became something called mshadow. It was a bit painful, honestly, but it gave me a feeling of full control. When you build from scratch, you can try ideas that don't fit neatly into an existing framework's assumptions. And a lot of those frameworks at the time were designed with a particular kind of model in mind, so if you wanted to do something a little different, you'd end up fighting the tool.

The other thing is that the learning compounds. Each time I built something, whether it was a model, a GPU kernel, or later XGBoost, I accumulated a set of building blocks and intuitions about systems. That eventually led me toward the realization that the real interesting problem isn't only the model, it's the infrastructure that makes the model possible. That's what pushed me into things like MXNet and later TVM. So in hindsight, building from scratch wasn't really about rejecting the existing tools. It was about learning the full stack, and that turned out to shape my whole research direction.

r001.rationale: The response says building from scratch gave Chen “full control” and let him try model ideas that did not fit existing frameworks’ assumptions, communicating control over how models were formulated.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it was just that I wanted to understand what was going on underneath. When I was at Shanghai Jiao Tong, and later at the University of Washington, deep learning was starting to get exciting again, and I remember looking at Theano and cuda-convnet and thinking, these are impressive, but I don't actually know why they work the way they do. Theano does this symbolic graph thing, compiles it, and out comes a gradient. That felt like magic, and I don't like relying on magic for something I'm supposed to be an expert in.

So I started writing my own convolutional network code, partly as an exercise. I wanted to write the CUDA kernels myself, figure out how the memory layout affects performance, see how backpropagation actually flows through each layer. Once you've done that by hand once, you have this mental model that lets you reason about everything else: why a certain operator is slow, why a model doesn't converge, where the bottleneck is. That is very hard to get if you only use a black box.

The second reason was more practical. Those early systems were built for a fairly narrow set of use cases. cuda-convnet was extremely fast, but it was Alex's code for Alex's problem, and it was hard to extend. Theano was flexible but compilation was slow and it was awkward to run across multiple GPUs. I was a student with limited GPUs, and I wanted to run things efficiently in ways those tools didn't quite support. When the existing tool doesn't fit, you have two options: bend your problem to the tool, or build the tool. I've always leaned toward the second.

And that habit carried over. XGBoost came from the same place: gradient boosting existed, but I wanted a version that was fast enough and scalable enough for the problems I had, so I wrote it. Later, with cxxnet and then MXNet and TVM, the same instinct. Building from scratch isn't about rejecting what came before. It's that building is how I learn, and once you understand something deeply you often find there's a better way to do it. A lot of the design decisions in MXNet, like mixing symbolic and imperative execution, came directly out of lessons from writing those early things myself and seeing where Theano-style pure symbolic programming got painful.

I'd also say there was a community aspect. At the time, a lot of us, students in Washington, CMU, NYU, were all writing our own little frameworks, and comparing notes. It wasn't that anybody thought their code would be the one everyone used. It was more a way of participating in the field. In hindsight that period of lots of people building from scratch was really productive, because the good ideas from all those experiments ended up getting merged into the frameworks people use today.

r001.rationale: The response says he built from scratch to understand implementation details and reason about performance and training behavior, but it does not identify control over model formulation as the reason.
